Governance

The comprehensive Group’s Sustainability Strategy and Programme has allowed SRLHANZ to be in a
fortunate position to respond to the introduction of climate reporting in NZ. SRLANZ will continue to
leverage and build on this position to ensure full compliance with the new reporting standards going
forward.

At the local level, the Board of Directors of SRLHA oversees climate-related risks and opportunities.
The Financial Condition Report for SRLHA which is approved by the local Board of Directors
specifically notes climate risk as an emerging and future potential risk and the topic is discussed at
the Board level. SRLHA also, leverage the Swiss Re's global Sustainability Strategy and expertise.
This achieves a centralised response to the global climate challenges, maximizing impact with shared
expertise and resources. Addressing climate change effectively requires coordinated action across all
our international operations. By pooling necessary resources from across the entire organisation
Swiss Re has access to research, expertise, and technologies unavailable to individual subsidiaries
and branches. This approach ensures both local relevance and global impact. Furthermore,
centralised governance ensures consistency, transparency and facilitates climate action across all
Swiss Re business units. Therefore, to ensure relevance for primary users of this report, the local
governance structure is followed by information on the Group level governance.

The Governance, Nomination and Sustainability Committee supports the Board with succession
planning at both the Board and Group EC level. It regularly reviews the qualifications and skills
represented on the Board, and ensures these are aligned with best practice, stakeholder demands
and changing business needs. It submits recommendations to the Board, which decides which
selection criteria are used to assess candidates for Board membership. The GNSC initiates the
evaluation of potential new Board members in a timely manner with the aim of ensuring the Board
maintains the desired expertise and experience and placing particular focus on gender diversity. See
the Swiss Re Sustainability Report 2023 at page 26 for further information on Board skills and

Swiss Re’s climate-related governance is part of its overall sustainability governance. Climate risk
mitigation and the energy transition are a core pillar of Swiss Re’s sustainability strategy since 2019.

Governance and Nomination and Sustainability Committee (GNSC) The GNSC regularly monitors
initiatives related to the Group Sustainability Strategy. It oversees the Group’s approach to
sustainability matters and related principles, and how they are embedded at all levels of the Group.
The GNSC keeps abreast of the GSC’s activities and oversees the integration of governance and
operational aspects of sustainability, including initiatives and actions specifically addressing climate
change.

Group Executive Committee (Group EC) While the Board of Directors is responsible for oversight,
implementation of the Group Sustainability Strategy is the responsibility of the Group EC. The Group
EC approves sustainability policies which apply locally to SRLHANZ. It also sets and monitors risk
capacity limits, including for natural catastrophes, and determines product policy as well as
underwriting and investment standards. In addition, the Group EC monitors operational progress in
the area of sustainability. The Group EC ensured the continued implementation of the Group
Sustainability Strategy 2023-2025. It also supported the development and publication of new mid-
term carbon targets for selected single-risk portfolios in underwriting.

Group Chief Executive Officer (Group CEO) — the Group CEO is responsible for overseeing the

commitments and Swiss Re's compensation-linked sustainability key performance indicators
framework. The Group CEO engages with external stakeholders to advance Swiss Re in leading
sustainability related organisations.

Strategy

Swiss Re’s underwriting, and investment activities and own operations are tied to the real economy
and consequently linked to the impacts the world economy has on climate change. Climate risk
mitigation and the energy transition are a core pillar of Swiss Re’s sustainability strategy since 2019.

Swiss Re and SRLHANZ deem the impact of climate change on its portfolios and strategy overall to be
limited and manageable. Climate change may trigger changes to Swiss Re and to the structure of its
globally diversified portfolio. With its established strategic process, Swiss Re can respond effectively
to such changes.

Swiss Re actively monitors and manages the relevant re/insurance portfolios that are potentially
exposed to physical and transition risks related to climate change. Such risks could impact demand
for re/insurance products as well as the profitability in the short, medium, and long term.

Locally SRLHANZ adheres to the Group Sustainability Strategy and the outcomes of the Group-level
materiality assessment process for potential climate-relates risks and opportunities.

Resilience under different climate scenarios

At Group level, scenario analyses for Life & Health confirmed Swiss Re’s view that climate change
does not pose a fundamental threat to the resilience of Swiss Re for its re/insurance risk taking in
the short, medium, and long-term. Locally SRHLANZ follows the same view outlined below.

Climate Scenarios

Swiss Re uses qualitative and quantitative scenario analyses to assess the resilience of its strategy
under different climate scenarios. The scenarios by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for
Greening the Financial System (NGFS) serve as the common narrative for the analysis of investment
and underwriting portfolios®. The NGFS scenarios incorporate different degrees of transition risks
along different paths of global warming in the selected orderly, disorderly, and hot house scenario:

¢ Orderly (Net Zero 2050, Below 2°C): Climate policies are introduced early and become
gradually more stringent. Physical and transition risks are both relatively low.

* Disorderly (Delayed transition, Divergent Net Zero): Climate policies are delayed or
divergent across countries and sectors. Emission reductions need to be sharper than in the
orderly scenario to limit warming to the same target. The result is higher transition risk.

¢ Hot house world (Current policies, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)): Some
climate policies are implemented in some jurisdictions, but global efforts to limit warming
are insufficient. This leads to severe physical risks including irreversible impacts.

The NGFS scenarios are linked to Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios, which
Swiss Re uses for natural catastrophe re/insurance®. Differences of the projected physical impacts
between RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 8.5 in the short to medium term (i.e., in the next ten years), but
also in the long term (i.e., 2050) are minor, however, a considerable divergence is expected for the
second half of the 21st century. Furthermore, there is significant uncertainty within a single scenario
(e.g., RCP 4.5), mainly caused by different modelling assumptions used in various climate models. To

Physical risk related to climate change could disrupt Swiss Re’s own operations due to increased
frequency of weather-related events affecting its office locations. Swiss Re does not expect any of its
office locations to be exposed to risk levels that would undermine their economic viability. The
Group can adjust its locations relatively easily as almost all the offices are rented. Robust and
regularly tested business continuity plans covering all locations are in place to mitigate the risk of
weather-related disruptions.

Transitional risks

Swiss Re does not consider the transition to a net-zero GHG emission economy a material financial
risk for its re/insurance business in the short, medium and long term. It expects to be able to
manage the associated risks effectively thanks to the established processes for reviewing
underwriting assumptions based on the most recent loss experiences and scientific findings, as well
as the annual renewal of contracts. By extension, this applies to SRLHANZ business.

Policy, legal, technology, market and reputational risks and their potential impact on insurance
liabilities are described in the table "Transition risks for the real economy and their potential
relevance for re/insurance underwriting" in the Swiss Re Sustainability Report 2023, page 66. It
includes the implications they may have for re/insurers in general.

Opportunities
The transition to a net-zero emissions economy offers business opportunities for Swiss Re across a

range of sectors such as power and energy, materials and processes, logistics and transport, and
agroforestry and food.

Swiss Re has developed an approach to benefit from transition opportunities in the short, medium,
and long term. This includes further developing existing business areas, such as renewable energy. In
addition, new technological segments have been identified and assessed in terms of re/insurance
market potential in the short, medium, and long term. Based on this assessment, business areas
have been prioritised for investments in research, and new business propositions will be developed.

Locally SRLHANZ focuses on low-risk investments like cash and government bonds, limiting exposure
to climate-related considerations in its capital deployment decisions. However, the Group actively
integrates climate risks and opportunities into its investment strategies through tools like Oil & Gas
Policy, Thermal Coal Policy and ESG Risk Tool. To learn more please refer to the "Climate Strategy"
chapter, "Investments" section of the Swiss Re Sustainability Report 2023, pages 72-76.

Current and anticipated impacts of climate-related risks and opportunities

Our dynamic business model prioritizes managing volatility in our portfolios, including potential
impacts stemming from climate change. While we currently assess physical and transitional climate
risks as immaterial for SRLHANZ, it remains committed to continuous evaluation and adaptation.

This ensures our model stays responsive to evolving market conditions and potential climate-related
risks in the future.

In this context, Swiss Re launched the CO2NetZero Programme for its operations®. The policy
consists of a dual strategy, namely reducing GHG emissions to the greatest extent as swiftly as
possible, and gradually moving from carbon avoidance to carbon removal to compensate the
remaining emissions in scope (Scope 1, Scope 2, and selected Scope 3 categories). Swiss Re’s
transition path to net zero for its operations consists of two phases, which are encompassed by the
CO2NetZero Programme: Phase 1 (near-term, until 2030) and Phase 2 (long-term, beyond 2030).

For information about Swiss Re's 2023 performance against targets please see "Sustainability Targets
and Progress in 2023" section of the Swiss Re Sustainability Report 2023 pages 18-19.

The Group has set a target to purchase and retire 100% carbon removal certificates as early as 2030,
covering the remaining operational emissions in scope in that year. Swiss Re continues to purchase
and retire carbon avoidance and carbon removal certificates to compensate its remaining
Operational emissions in scope for the near-term, linearly increasing the minimum share of carbon
removal certificates in the mix from 0% in 2020 to 100% in 2030. Following an internal standard on
carbon certificates purchase, Swiss Re assesses key quality aspects such as integrity, durability,
scalability, and additional social co-benefits to determine the overall quality of carbon certificates.
To learn more about Swiss Re's approach to carbon removal and avoidance certificate sourcing and
retirement as well as certificates used for emissions compensation in 2023, please refer to Swiss Re's
roach to using carbon certificates | Swiss Re website®,

In early 2021, Swiss Re became the first multinational company to introduce an ambitious triple-digit
real internal carbon price on both direct and indirect operational GHG emissions. It covers all Scope
1, all Scope 2 (market-based) and a significant part of upstream Scope 3 emissions (i.e., business
travel, fuel and energy-related activities, paper, water, and waste) across all the Group’s Business
Units, functions, and locations. The carbon steering levy, Swiss Re’s internal carbon price on both
direct and indirect operational GHG emissions was set at NZD 194” in 2023 up from NZD 177" in
2022. This increase is part of the plan to gradually raise the levy to NZD 316” per tonne of CO2e by
2030, which reflects the expected market price for high-quality carbon removal certificates at that
point in time. (See chapter " Sustainable Operations", "The Internal Carbon Steering Levy" section of
the Swiss Re Sustainability Report 2023 page 91 for further details).

SRLHANZ actively contributes to the Group's overall GHG emission reduction strategy. SRLHANZ has
an annual CO2 emissions budget targeting business travel (commercial flights). This budget aligns
with Swiss Re's overarching GHG reduction targets, ensuring all business units and functions
contribute to achieving the shared goals.

In 2023, SRLHANZ branch's operational GHG emissions totalled 4.46 tonnes CO2e, including Scope 1
emissions 880 kg CO2e, Scope 2 market-based emissions 32 kg CO2e, location-based 3544 kg CO2e.
GHG emissions are estimated using FTE intensities as a proxy.
